findings.where: Puzzles, steps 4, 6, 8, 11, 12 and 13 (the receipt, order, reading and fact cards)
findings.what: Before Dan answers, every card already prints its fact's equation (for example 4s + 2w = 22, y − x = 6, and 100a + b = 20 and 400a + b = 50 on 360-light-end). So the skill this lesson is named for, turning words into equations, is done for him on every puzzle except step 2. And because dragging the ring to any answer shows 'passes both', each puzzle can be solved by guess-and-check on the grid, the habit step 4 tells him to drop. Show 'Its equation: ?' on these cards until Check or Why?, as step 2 already does.

Three items are listed as common mistakes with no source counting them: 'Swapping which letter stands for which thing', 'Writing 2 bags of popcorn as p + 2' and 'Forcing a machine's law through zero'. The brief puts letter-swapping under 'Not stated as common ... taught as checks, not as cited mistakes'. Keep the sourced items under the heading (using one fact only, stopping at the numbers) and move these three under something like 'Slips to check for'.

findings.where: Step 4 'Work it out' and step 10 'Something new'
findings.what: Step 4 asks for the drink and popcorn prices that step 3 has just shown ('Both pass (£3, £2)', 'Means: a drink costs £3'), so Dan can answer from memory without working anything out. Step 10's three receipts are the same ones steps 3 and 9 have just judged. Fresh receipts would make him solve: for example, 2 drinks and 1 bag for £6.50 and 1 drink and 2 bags for £5.50 give a £2.50 drink and £1.50 popcorn, both on the 50p grid.

findings.where: Step 5 'Two orders of cable' and step 7 'A machine's law', demonstrations (contact sheets s4 and s6)
findings.what: The guess travels straight to the answer at 1.4 to 2.0 s, before either line arrives (2.2 and 2.5 s) and before the 'Take away' row (3.0 s). The motion therefore shows the answer as already known before it is worked out, which runs against 'work it out instead'. Bring the Take away and Put back rows in first, then move the guess to the pair they give.

findings.where: Step 4 'Work it out', the Solve row after the answer or Why?, and the explain's second paragraph
findings.what: '−3d = 7 − 16 = −9, so d = 3' leaves out dividing by −3. subRows only writes the division when the coefficient is above 1. Write 'so d = −9 ÷ −3 = 3'.

The screen says every accepted guess lands on one straight line but not why. The explain gives the reason: each £1 more on the drink must come off as £2 less on the popcorn. The demonstration's stops, (£2, £4) to (£3, £2) to (£1, £6), show exactly that step, so one sentence on the screen would give the cause where the line appears.

findings.where: Receipt cards on every screen, the 'too much' / 'too little' status (red 'too little' on 360-light-end before any answer)
findings.what: When a fact does not fit a guess, the card shows its status in warning red even though Dan has made no mistake; on the puzzles this happens to the starting guess. The brief says a rule a point does not fit shows in ink 'because exploring is not a mistake'. Keep red for the wrong-equation card on step 2.

findings.where: Second fact's line, marks and key swatch on every screen
findings.what: The second fact is drawn in teal (--k-accent). The brief decided that every line is ink, told apart by solid and dashed, with colour kept for meaning. This was raised on lesson 1 too.

findings.where: All puzzles, against the brief's 'Every DO screen asks what the pair means, with its unit'
findings.what: No puzzle asks what a solved pair means. The meaning shows only in the 'Means' row after Check, although 'unable to interpret solutions in context' is the sourced mistake this lesson was meant to catch. One puzzle could offer three readings of P = 0.08W + 10, for example '10 N is the effort with no load' against '10 N per newton of load'.
'a = 0.08, b = 10' gives b without its unit, in the lesson that asks for units every time. The Guess line already writes 'b = 15 N', so write 'b = 10 N' on the buttons too.

findings.where: Step 13 'Last one', wrong picks 25 N and 50 N
findings.what: Dan picks an effort, but the working's first row reads 'Tried (0.1, 0)' or '(0.2, 0)', a pair he never chose. Label that row so it links the effort to the law behind it, for example '25 N comes from a = 0.1, b = 0'.

findings.where: Steps 5 to 13, each story's first sentence
findings.what: Only the step 1 lead says the stories use example figures, and the lead is hidden from step 2 on. The machine readings (steps 7, 8, 13) and the prices (steps 5, 6, 12) carry no label on their own screens, but the brief asks for one. Add 'example' to each story's first sentence, for example 'Two example readings'.

findings.where: Step 9 'The same fact twice' at £15 (contact sheet s8), and step 10's third receipt
findings.what: At £15 the dashed line is only 50p below the solid one, about 9 px apart at 360 px, so it reads as nearly on top rather than plainly alongside. It also makes the halved receipt '2d + p = 7.50'. At £14 the gap doubles and the halved receipt reads '2d + p = 7, but receipt 1 says 8'.
'Drag the ring, or use the arrow keys' sits below Continue at the very foot of the page on a phone, far from the grid. The key's 'guess' could read 'guess (drag it)' so the cue sits next to the ring.
